column1: What determines whether division is integer or floating-point?
column2:
The operand types after arithmetic conversions, not the destination type. Converting the result afterward cannot restore a discarded fractional part.

double a = 7 / 2;   // 3.0
double b = 7.0 / 2; // 3.5

column1: How do prefixes determine the base of an integer literal in C++?
column2:
No prefix means decimal; a leading 0 means octal; 0b means binary; 0x means hexadecimal. All of the following have the same value.

10
012
0b1010
0xA

column1: How does brace initialization protect against narrowing conversions?
column2:
Brace initialization rejects narrowing conversions. Ordinary copy initialization can allow them, potentially losing information.

int a = 3.7; // allowed: a becomes 3
int b{3.7};  // error: narrowing
double c{3}; // OK: exactly representable

column1: Does auto make a variable dynamically typed?
column2:
No. Its type is deduced at declaration and stays fixed. Later assignments convert to that type when the conversion is permitted.

auto value = 10; // int
value = 2.8;     // still int; value becomes 2

column1: How do const and constexpr differ for variables?
column2:
const allows runtime initialization and prevents modification through that name. A constexpr object is also const, but requires a constant-expression initializer.

const int a = ReadInput(); // runtime input is allowed
constexpr int b = 2 * 3;   // constant expression required

column1: Must a constexpr function always execute at compile time?
column2:
No. It can participate in constant expressions, but it can also execute at runtime. A constexpr variable requires its initializer to satisfy constant-expression rules.

constexpr int Twice(int x) { return x * 2; }
constexpr int a = Twice(3); // constant evaluation required
int b = Twice(ReadInput()); // runtime input

column1: Is an expression a constant expression just because the optimizer computes it in advance?
column2:
No. Constant expressions must satisfy language rules. Optimization can precompute other expressions without making them valid in contexts requiring a constant expression.

int Twice(int x) { return x * 2; }
int a = Twice(3);           // optimizer may replace with 6
constexpr int b = Twice(3); // error: function is not constexpr

column1: How do value and reference loop variables affect vector<int> elements?
column2:
A value loop variable is a copy; modifying it leaves the vector unchanged. A reference loop variable refers to the original element. For read-only access to small scalar types, copying is usually appropriate.

for (auto x : values) ++x;        // modifies copies
for (auto& x : values) ++x;       // modifies elements
for (auto x : values) Print(x);  // reads copies

column1: Does iterating by reference allocate a separate pointer for every vector element?
column2:
No array of pointers is created. The loop binds a reference to the current element on each iteration. References do not necessarily need separate storage; exact register or stack usage depends on generated code.

for (auto it = values.begin(); it != values.end(); ++it) {
    int& x = *it;
    ++x;
} // no per-element pointer collection

std::string source = "hello";
std::string destination = std::move(source); // move construction
// Do not assume a moved-from string is empty.

column1: What is guaranteed about a unique_ptr after its ownership is moved to another unique_ptr?
column2:
The destination owns the object and the source is empty (nullptr). This is a unique_ptr guarantee, not a general rule for every moved-from type.

auto source = std::make_unique<int>(42);
auto destination = std::move(source);
// source == nullptr
// *destination == 42

column1: Why is initializer_list problematic for a vector of move-only objects?
column2:
Its elements are exposed as const. The vector must construct its own elements from them. Typical ownership-transferring moves cannot modify a const source, and move-only types cannot be copied.

std::vector<std::unique_ptr<int>> values{
    std::make_unique<int>(42)
}; // error
// std::move inside the braces does not solve this.

column1: What is copied when a shared_ptr is copied, and when should shared_ptr be chosen?
column2:
Copying a shared_ptr shares ownership of the same object; it does not copy that object. Choose shared_ptr when multiple owners need to control lifetime together, not just to make initializer_list syntax work.

auto a = std::make_shared<int>(42);
auto b = a;
// a and b own the same int
*b = 7; // *a is now 7

column1: What is object slicing, and how do base references or pointers avoid it?
column2:
Copying a derived object into a concrete base object retains only the base portion. A base reference or pointer refers to the original derived object, allowing virtual dispatch to use its actual type.

Derived derived;
Base copy = derived; // slicing, if Base is concrete
Base& ref = derived; // refers to the original object
// If Base is abstract, constructing copy is forbidden.

column1: Why does a polymorphic owning base class need a virtual destructor?
column2:
When deleting a derived object through a base pointer, a virtual base destructor ensures the derived destructor runs before the base destructor. With ordinary delete, deleting through a base pointer without a virtual destructor is undefined behavior.

struct Base {
    virtual ~Base() = default;
};
struct Derived : Base {};
std::unique_ptr<Base> p = std::make_unique<Derived>();
// Default deletion through Base* is safe.
